themes.title: State transitions
mainQuestions: With settings 20, 80, 100, walk me through what your controller does for the readings 50, 18, 40, 85, 70, 15, and how many times the pump starts.
criteria: The student traces each reading to the correct state and explains why the state holds between the two levels.

rubric.text: At 40 the controller stays `FILLING`, because a reading between `low` and `high` keeps the current state.
At 70 the controller stays `FULL` for the same reason (it does not go back to `IDLE` or `FILLING`).
The pump starts twice (at 18 and at 15), because a start is counted only when entering `FILLING` from another state.

themes.title: Design reasoning
mainQuestions: Why does the controller use two levels, 20 and 80, instead of switching the pump at a single level like 50?
criteria: The student explains the purpose of the gap between the levels (hysteresis) and its effect on the pump.

rubric.text: With a single level, readings that go back and forth around it (49, 51, 49, 51) would turn the pump on and off on every reading.
The gap between the levels means the pump runs until the tank is high, and stays off until it is low, so it switches rarely.
Fewer switches means less wear on the pump (and a more stable level), which is why real controllers do this.

themes.title: Edge cases
mainQuestions: Suppose the controller is FILLING and the next reading is -5. What happens, and what happens with the readings after that?
criteria: The student explains how an invalid reading is detected and what the alarm state does to later readings.

rubric.text: -5 is invalid because it is negative, so the controller moves to `ALARM`.
The pump turns off in `ALARM` (it is not `FILLING` any more).
The controller stays in `ALARM` for every later reading, even valid ones, because `step` checks `ALARM` first.

themes.title: Boundaries and fault injection
mainQuestions: If the check `reading >= s.high` were changed to `reading > s.high`, what would change in the output?
criteria: The student identifies the boundary case the change affects and its consequence.

rubric.text: Only a reading of exactly 80 (exactly `high`) behaves differently.
An input that shows it, for example `10 80`: the second line becomes `80 -> FILLING` instead of `80 -> FULL`.
The pump keeps running at the high level, so the tank fills past the level it should stop at.

themes.title: Functions and state
mainQuestions: Your `step` function takes the current state and returns the next one, instead of changing a global variable. Why is that a useful way to write it?
criteria: The student explains the benefit of a pure function for a state machine.

rubric.text: It can be tested on its own: call it with any state and reading and check the result.
There is no hidden state, so the same inputs always give the same next state.
`main` stays in control of the current state, which makes the loop easy to read and trace.

fixedFollowUps: What does your controller print for the reading 70 right after the reading 85?
What would the pump do if the readings kept going 49, 51, 49, 51 with a single level at 50?
What does step return for a reading of 50 when current is ALARM?
What does your controller print for a reading of exactly 80 after a reading of 10?
How would you test step on its own, without running main?
